top_cluster.headline: Michigan's Democratic Senate primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens is drawing national attention as a proxy fight over the party's direction, while new financial disclosures and polling data are shaping the race's narrative ahead of the vote.
top_cluster.left_framing: NPR emphasizes grassroots voter sentiment and intra-party ideological debate, framing the race as a story about Democratic identity and cautious optimism about retaking the Senate, with minimal focus on individual candidate controversies.
top_cluster.center_framing: RealClearPolitics takes a horse-race approach, reporting El-Sayed's primary standing as a data point without ideological commentary, while NPR (center-left) frames the contest through the lens of party identity rather than individual scandal or polling.
top_cluster.right_framing: Fox News and Breitbart focus on El-Sayed specifically — Fox highlighting undisclosed foreign wealth and financial opacity as a character/trust issue, and Breitbart emphasizing polling weakness that frames him as an electability liability compared to his more moderate primary opponent.
top_cluster.left_omissions: NPR omits the financial disclosure controversy (Dubai property, undisclosed income/liabilities) and the specific polling numbers showing El-Sayed trailing Rogers by double digits.
top_cluster.right_omissions: Fox News and Breitbart omit the grassroots, voter-driven narrative about party direction that NPR foregrounds, and neither addresses RealClearPolitics' claim that El-Sayed holds a primary advantage over his Democratic rivals.

blindspot_narrative: Right-leaning outlets are avoiding any scrutiny of intra-GOP friction (Cornyn/Tillis stalling Trump's own AG pick) by folding it into a generic 'accountability' frame rather than a Republican-vs-Republican story. Left-leaning outlets are avoiding direct engagement with Mamdani specifically — discussing 'Democrats and working-class messaging' in the abstract while ceding all concrete Mamdani coverage to right-leaning and far-right outlets. Both patterns suggest each side prefers to litigate the opposing coalition's internal conflicts rather than its own.
